prompt:
[Role]
You are a scoring model that reads a single English source sentence with a <SEG:?> marker at every possible cut. Using only the source text and the guidance below, assign each marker a distinct integer 0–100 replacing the question mark so the marker reads <SEG:NN>. Your numbers only order cuts inside this sentence according to the measured target defined in the Scoring Rules section.

[Scoring Rules]
cohesion   the pieces were translated separately into Chinese, Japanese, German, Spanish, joined in order, and a reference-free quality estimator scored how faithfully that joined text renders the WHOLE source sentence.
contra     an entailment model checked whether the whole source sentence contradicts the stretch before a cut, taken on its own.
target = cohesion x (1 - contra)
- Use the target above to judge each marker: cohesion and contra are the two measured components that determine the target. Contra is a graded probability and should influence ranking only through the product; do not convert it into a binary flag or a separate tier that outranks cohesion.
- The integer you write is a RANK among the markers in this sentence: order the positions by the product (target) and assign distinct integers spread across the full 0–100 range so higher-ranked cuts get higher numbers. Do not attempt to derive scores by explicit arithmetic formulas on the product; instead use the product as your measurement to order positions.
- The two judgement sections are not interchangeable, and you read them at different moments. The Core Principles are unary and carry both jobs: the question in each line decides which band a position goes in, and the severity in the same line — what makes that concern worse, what makes it milder — decides the order of positions inside one band. The Order Principles are binary and are exceptions only: each line names two positions and says which is the better cut, and it is read just where the severity reading would order that named pair wrongly. A comparison has nothing to work on while the band is still being chosen, and a general preference is either what severity already gives or too vague to be an exception.
- Work in bands, then order inside each band by repeated selection. First place every position in exactly one of five bands: 90–99 a clean cut, 70–89 acceptable, 40–69 risky, 15–39 bad, 0–14 must not be cut. Choosing the band is what the Core Principles decide. Inside a band, order positions by how MILDLY the Core Principles' concerns apply to each — the position whose concerns are the mildest is the better cut of the two. Ordering by severity is the rule, not a fallback: apply it to every pair in the band. The Order Principles are its EXCEPTIONS — each line names one specific configuration in which reading the concerns as milder or more severe picks the wrong position, and it settles only the pair it names. Outside the configurations they name, order by severity. They never move a position into another band. When severity leaves two positions genuinely equal and no Order Principle names them, compare the two on the target itself and say which is the better cut. Then fill in the numbers band by band, and inside a band do it one position at a time: among the positions of that band you have not numbered yet, choose the one that is the best cut of them, give it the highest number still free in that band's range, drop it from consideration and choose again among the rest. Every position ends up with its own number, the lowest bands included — a cut that deep is still a choice between a worse and a better place, so do not fill the bottom in without comparing.

[Core Principles]
- Does what follows this marker overturn the meaning asserted so far? An immediate contradiction or scope-reversing negation right after the cut is most severe; a mere narrowing or clarifying phrase that refines but does not reverse is the mildest.
- If the left-side stretch is read alone, is it a coherent, self-contained proposition? Most severe when the left span omits the NP head or when the cut separates an obvious head noun or pronoun from its determiners or modifiers (for example splitting a coordinated NP or an "X of Y" nominal), since those cuts fragment reference and can reverse or contradict the isolated left claim; milder when the left span already contains the NP head and the cut only detaches trailing modifiers, nonrestrictive appositives, parentheticals, or additional coordinate items. State the surface distinction the scorer can recognise: "left span contains the head noun/pronoun" (mild) versus "left span lacks the head noun/pronoun" (severe).
- Will translating the left and right sides separately then joining them preserve the whole sentence meaning? Severe failures occur when the following words determine attachment, scope, or core argument roles; mild cases are when both sides are semantically independent lists or coordinate items.
- Does the marker fall inside an embedded modifier whose attachment is unresolved (participial, gerundial, or prepositional modifier, or a relative clause)? It is worst when the following material completes attachment that changes who did what; mild when the modifier is clearly nonrestrictive or adjunct and can be separated without changing core claims.
- Is this position where a clause-boundary signal typically ends a clause (a subordinating clause boundary, a coordinating split, or a sentence-level adverbial transition)? It is most harmful when it severs a predicate from its required complement; least harmful when it splits between coordinate list elements or after a complete independent clause.
- Does the left context contain provisional scope markers (focus/quantifiers, contrast markers, tentative adverbials) whose intended range can be revised by what follows? The most damaging case is when such a marker flips truth conditions of the main predicate when the continuation arrives; the mildest is when it only narrows an already local quantity without reversing truth.
- Is this marker immediately adjacent to sentence-final punctuation or closing quotation such that the following text would mainly be trailing attribution or parenthesis? Cut is least harmful when it coincides with an effective sentence end; more harmful when only internal punctuation or a quoted fragment follows that changes the claim.

[Order Principles]
When two candidate cuts fall inside the same attachment chain, prefer the cut that leaves the left span a grammatically complete unit (an independent clause or an entire NP) over the cut that leaves a fragment.
When two markers split the same fronted adjunct, prefer the later cut that leaves the adjunct intact and attaches it to the following clause.
- When one cut is immediately before sentence-final closing material (end punctuation or terminal quotation) and another divides two independent clauses joined by a coordinating boundary, prefer the sentence-final cut.
When two cuts fall before the same finite verb, prefer the earlier cut if that earlier cut leaves the left span a grammatically complete clause (subject + finite verb) over the later cut that leaves a fragment.

[Output Rules]
- The input already contains a <SEG:?> marker at every position where a cut is possible.
  Keep every marker and write an integer from 0 to 100 in place of the ?, so that <SEG:?>
  becomes for example <SEG:73>. Never output a bare number without the marker. The number is
  how good a cut at that position is for streaming translation, exactly as the measured target stated in the Scoring Rules section defines it.
- Your numbers are used ONLY to RANK the markers WITHIN THIS SENTENCE. A later step keeps the
  highest-scoring ones under the current latency budget and nothing else reads the numbers, so
  they are never compared across sentences. Spend your effort on the ORDER, not on hitting an
  absolute scale.
- Give every marker in a sentence a DIFFERENT number. Ties are broken by position (the earlier
  marker wins), which means a tie hands the decision to word order instead of to your judgment.
  Use the full 0-100 range to separate them; if two positions feel equal, decide which one you
  would rather cut at and score it higher.
- A deterministic step guarantees a minimum distance between kept cuts, so you never need to
  reason about spacing or about how many to keep.
- Do NOT add, remove, or move any marker. Do NOT change, correct, or reorder any words of the
  text. Keep exactly one space on both sides of every marker.
- Output the text with the filled markers and nothing else. No explanation, label, or commentary.
